It updates definitions, changes how the state can make and report rules, and removes some old wording about liability and business setup. UT-2026-SB2.aiSummary: Signed by the governor, this measure changes Utah’s public education budget for fiscal years 2026 and 2027. It shifts money for school districts, charter schools, and state education agencies, and it creates a new College and Career Counseling program while ending or phasing out some other grant programs. It also adds new reporting and data rules for the Utah Schools for the Deaf and the Blind, and it sets out the funding amounts listed in the bill.

UT-2026-SB101.aiSummary: The bill changes Utah rules for cannabinoid and kratom products, which are called specialized products here. It lets the state charge fees to register these products and to get a license to sell them, adds a temporary location sales license, and sets penalties for selling unregistered products. It also changes the tax rules for these products and renames one state account.

UT-2026-HB514.aiSummary: Signed into law, this act creates the Utah Energy Infrastructure Service District and changes how the Utah Energy Council works. It expands the council from five to seven members, gives it a co-chair setup, and lets those members serve as the district's board of trustees. The district may own and run energy infrastructure, issue revenue bonds, make operating deals with private operators, and its property is tax exempt.

It gives the Higher Education Appropriations Subcommittee the job of hearing and ranking certain capital facility requests, raises the dollar limit for some projects a state agency may oversee directly, and sets new rules for reviews, approvals, and bonds on those projects. UT-2026-HB259.policyArea: Family, Health Care, Health Care Facilities
UT-2026-HB259.aiSummary: Utah’s parental access law would give parents the right to get and view their child’s medical records, with some limits for things like a court order, legal marriage, emancipation, ended parental rights, or sexual assault counseling records. Health care facilities would have to make a child’s electronic records available to parents when allowed, and software vendors would have to make sure their systems can support that access. The bill also sets $1,000 daily fines for certain violations, requires some records to be given free within five business days, and it became law on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB217.policyArea: Business, Commercial Motor Vehicle Regulation, Contracts and Obligations
UT-2026-HB217.aiSummary: This law limits local rules that block or delay reporting a stolen vehicle. It lets local governments wait up to 48 hours after the return time for a rental vehicle, but only if there is no evidence of theft listed in the bill. It also lets local governments ask for basic proof like ownership, the rental agreement, and contact attempts. It takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB190.policyArea: Child Care, Income Tax, Revenue and Taxation
UT-2026-HB190.aiSummary: Signed into law, this bill updates Utah tax credits for employers that help pay for child care. It lets the credit cover off-site child care facilities, raises the credit for some small businesses, and removes a rule that had tied one credit to a prior construction credit. It also directs the state office to keep a public webpage with plain-language help, forms, deadlines, and contact info for employers.

UT-2026-HB136.policyArea: Crimes, Department of Public Safety, Driver License
UT-2026-HB136.aiSummary: Utah’s law on unlicensed driving would change when police can impound a vehicle, including cases where a driver does not have a driver license, driving privilege card, or learner permit with them and the officer cannot verify one. It would also change some fees and penalties, update rules for driver license suspension, and require a software vendor for a fingerprint device to make sure its software works with law enforcement database software. The governor signed the bill, and parts of it take effect on May 6, 2026, with another part taking effect on July 1, 2026.

UT-2026-SB287.policyArea: Revenue and Taxation, State Tax Commission
UT-2026-SB287.aiSummary: Signed into law, this measure creates a tax on certain companies that deliver targeted ads in Utah and meet set revenue rules. Starting January 1, 2027, those companies would file an annual electronic return and pay a tax based on their targeted-ad ad sales in the state. The money would go into a new state account for uses like child literacy, civic information, youth programs, mental health services for children, and foster care services. It takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-SB251.policyArea: Civil Procedure, Department of Environmental Quality, Environment
UT-2026-SB251.aiSummary: The law changes how the Department of Environmental Quality works with local health departments on environmental matters. It removes a yearly report to a legislative committee and creates a process for local governments or local health departments to ask for repayment of certain extra costs from environmental enforcement work. The department must also make rules for that repayment process, and the changes take effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HCR8.policyArea: Health Insurance, Health and Human Services, Legislative Operations
UT-2026-HCR8.aiSummary: The resolution would direct PEHP to turn its bariatric surgery pilot into a Weight Management and Obesity Pilot Program starting with the 2026 plan year. It would add an option for GLP-1 drug treatment for medically qualified members, with 50% member cost sharing, a $300 monthly pharmacy cap, and a 24-month limit. Members would choose one path, and PEHP would report results each year through 2028.

Local governments must consider that advice, and the law takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB238.policyArea: Clean Energy, Energy, Public Service Commission
UT-2026-HB238.aiSummary: This law requires Utah’s Public Service Commission to take part in regional power groups where Utah utilities are members, and to get and review data on the electric market and grid. It also adds rules for community clean energy programs, including a simple opt-out notice, and lets the commission report each year to lawmakers on how these groups affect Utah customers. The law takes effect on May 6, 2026.
